documents.abstract: La incorporación de tecnologías digitales en la educación superior no garantiza por sí sola transformaciones pedagógicas significativas si no está acompañada de una reflexión didáctica crítica sobre sus finalidades y modos de uso. En este marco, esta investigación analiza la incorporación de materiales didácticos interactivos autoadministrados, diseñados con apoyo de inteligencia artificial (IA), según el modelo de sustitución, aumento, modificación y redefinición (SAMR) y en clave problematizadora, en comparación con clases presenciales tradicionales, en el curso introductorio de la Facultad de Información y Comunicación (FIC) de la Universidad de la República (Udelar) de Uruguay. Este curso es obligatorio para todo el estudiantado de ingreso, tiene como propósito ofrecer información sobre la oferta formativa de la FIC, su estructura académica, instalaciones y espacios de referencia institucionales. La intervención, dirigida a 1254 estudiantes inscritos de las licenciaturas en Comunicación, Archivología y Bibliotecología, consistió en sustituir las presentaciones presenciales iniciales de las unidades curriculares del primer semestre por un módulo virtual interactivo que integró múltiples lenguajes, navegación condicionada, un espacio colaborativo asíncrono y una encuesta de retroalimentación. El diseño promovió un recorrido autónomo y progresivo del contenido, habilitando la reflexión individual y colectiva. Se recogieron 831 respuestas a la encuesta (66.3 %) y 628 publicaciones en el espacio colaborativo (50.1 %). Esto permitió evaluar percepciones, niveles de apropiación conceptual y evidencias de autorregulación. Los resultados sugieren que la propuesta contribuye a fomentar la autonomía estudiantil y a enriquecer los procesos de enseñanza en educación superior mediante el uso crítico y pedagógico de tecnologías digitales.[The integration of digital technologies in higher education does not automatically lead to meaningful pedagogical transformation unless it is guided by critical reflection on their educational purposes and uses. This research analyzes the integration of self-paced interactive learning materials designed with the support of artificial intelligence (AI), following the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) model and framed from a problematizing approach. It compares these materials with traditional face-to-face classes within the introductory course at the Faculty of Information and Communication (FIC), Universidad de la República, Uruguay (Udelar). This mandatory course is aimed at all first-year students and seeks to provide information about the FIC’s academic offerings, academic structure, facilities, and institutional reference spaces. The intervention, targeting 1,254 enrolled students from the Communication, Archival Science, and Library Science programs, involved replacing the initial in-person presentations of first-semester courses with an interactive virtual module. This module incorporated multiple media, conditional navigation, an asynchronous collaborative space, and a feedback survey. The design encouraged a self-guided and progressive exploration of content, enabling both individual and collective reflection. A total of 831 responses to the survey (66.3%) and 628 posts in the collaborative space (50.1%) were collected, allowing for the evaluation of perceptions, conceptual appropriation levels, and evidence of self-regulated learning. The results suggest that this initiative helps foster student autonomy and enriches teaching processes in higher education through the critical and pedagogical use of digital technologies].

Skin conditions are among the most common reasons patients seek medical attention worldwide, ranging from self-limiting infections to chronic, disfiguring, or malignant disease. Although deep learning models for dermatological image classification frequently report high overall accuracy, this metric often conceals critical performance failures on clinically vulnerable minority classes such as cancer. To address this, we propose a hybrid classification framework combining DenseNet121 and EfficientNetB0 architectures with transformer-based feature fusion, trained on a DermNet-derived corpus of clinical photographs. Furthermore, we implement a multi-method post- hoc explainability protocol comparing input-gradient saliency, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME). The framework was evaluated on a held-out test set of 897 images, measuring overall accuracy, balanced accuracy, and cancer recall alongside cross- method attribution consistency on misclassified cases. The results demonstrate that a high overall accuracy of 91.0% masked a severe cancer recall deficit of 40.0%, whereas multi-method explainability exposed shortcut learning vulnerabilities, with SHAP partially attributing decisions to image watermarks. This work contributes evidence that single-number accuracy and single-method explanations are insufficient, and it supports disaggregated performance reporting and multi-method explanation as minimum requirements for reliable clinical artificial intelligence (AI) evaluation

Abstract A growing body of research on board games demonstrates that these games can function as learning environments and provide opportunities for learning across diverse contexts. Although learning is often conceptualized contextually within this literature, studies increasingly demonstrate that meaningful learning can occur through participation in board game environments. However, the relationship between board games and learning has been examined predominantly through the study of modern board games, with comparatively limited attention given to classic African board games. This literature review explores learning in classic African board games. This study serves two purposes as it highlights the state of research on classic African board games and the relationship of these games with learning. The fi ndings show that classic African board games are spaces where learning occurs and players engage in a constellation of literacies. The studies analyzed indicate that playing these games can facilitate mathematical learning, engage players in computational thinking and songoputation, and foster the development of skills related to science, engineering, and technology (i.e. STEM). These board games also allow for the exploration of artificial intelligence (AI), which results in the learning of new AI techniques. Classic African board games have the potential to simplify the learning of various subjects and the acquisition of skills relevant to the 21st century. As such, more empirical studies should be conducted to further investigate the connection between playing thesegames, their game mechanics and learning; and particularly the link between their gameplay and the learning of specific subjects such as mathematics, science, and engineering.
topics: Physical education and sports games research

documents.abstract: Effective communication is essential in nursing, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly integrated into nursing education. This phenomenological study explores how ChatGPT-supported virtual patient scenarios influence nursing students’ empathy and communication skills. Third-year nursing students enrolled in a Family Health Nursing elective interacted with a virtual patient through predefined ChatGPT prompts simulating a counseling session. Data were collected through focus group interviews and online reflective diaries. Thematic analysis revealed three themes: “Unrealistic empathy and communication experience”, “Solution-oriented and effective communication experience”, “Communication and empathy awareness: Future communication strategies and professional preparation” Although participants perceived ChatGPT-supported virtual patient communication as providing a less realistic communication and empathy experience than real patient interactions, they also reported that ChatGPT’s interaction style offered a structured and solution-oriented communication experience. Furthermore, the ChatGPT-supported virtual patient communication experience was perceived as helping students make reflection and self-assessment about communication and empathy, and identify areas for improvement before interacting with real patients. These findings suggest that ChatGPT-supported virtual patient communication cannot replace real patient encounters, but it can serve as a complementary educational tool that encourages reflective learning and prepares nursing students for subsequent clinical communication experiences.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and metaverse on academic and personal growth of students, moderated by the components of social–emotional learning (SEL), that is, emotional intelligence and peer relationships. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a two-stage hybrid structural equation modeling (SEM) artificial neural network (ANN) methodology. The initial phase uses SmartPLS4 to perform partial least squares SEM for exploratory investigations. Further, to explore the non-linear interaction between variables, an ANN model is used. Findings Findings suggest that perceived usefulness significantly impacts academic growth. The relationship is enhanced by moderators such as peer relationships and emotional intelligence, where higher perceived usefulness weakens the contribution of peer relationships to personal growth, while emotional intelligence strengthens the contribution of perceived usefulness to personal growth. Moreover, the study identifies social–emotional variables as key predictors of enhanced personal and academic growth. Research limitations/implications This study offers major implications for higher education by demonstrating how integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and SEL frameworks can enhance students’ academic and personal growth. Practically, it urges institutions to prioritize emotional intelligence and peer relationships alongside technological adoption, promoting a more inclusive, sustainable and student-centered learning environment. Originality/value This study examines the use of emerging technologies, AI and metaverse applications in higher education. Its contribution lies in integrating them with the SEL framework. Rather than treating learner characteristics as predictors, this study positions emotional intelligence and peer relationships as moderators that influence whether technology engagement leads to academic and personal growth. By further modeling non-linear relationships among variables, this study refines the predictive understanding of technology-enhanced learning and informs the andragogical implementation of these tools.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming teaching and learning in accounting education. While AI technologies offer opportunities to enhance learning outcomes, academic performance is also influenced by broader educational factors such as teacher competence, institutional support, curriculum design, and student engagement. This study investigates the role of AI and educational factors in shaping academic performance in accounting education through a systematic literature review of studies published between 2020 and 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a structured search of major academic databases yielded 168 initial records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 28 studies were retained for final analysis. The review synthesizes empirical evidence on AI applications in accounting education and identifies key factors influencing student performance. The study is grounded in Human Capital Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, which provide insights into how technological and educational investments influence learning outcomes. The findings reveal that AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI tools, predictive analytics, and automated assessment platforms enhance academic performance through personalized learning and data-driven feedback. However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on teacher digital competence, student motivation, curriculum alignment, and institutional support. The study proposes an integrated conceptual framework linking AI adoption and educational factors to academic performance in accounting education. The findings provide implications for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers seeking to improve accounting education in the digital era.

Artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses systems engineered to execute cognitive functions, including perception, reasoning, and decision-making. Advancements in big data and deep learning have facilitated the proliferation of AI in sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, and transportation, concurrently prompting discussions on ethical and safety concerns. AI enhances education by facilitating personalized and data-informed learning via adaptive platforms, automated assessments, and virtual assistants. This study examined vocational school students' perceptions of AI using metaphors, which elucidate abstract concepts and uncover cognitive patterns. A qualitative, phenomenological approach was employed to collect data from 198 students through an online survey utilizing the prompt “AI is like… because…”. The analysis adhered to systematic metaphor procedures, and expert review validated a high degree of reliability. The results revealed 82 distinct metaphors that represent diverse perspectives. The recurrent use of metaphors such as “human,” “human brain,” “assistant,” and “facilitation” suggests that students perceive AI as possessing human-like qualities and as a supportive entity. Alternative metaphors characterize AI as technological instruments (robots, machines, programs) or repositories of information (libraries, web browsers). In addition to the beneficial aspects of assistance and facilitation, apprehensions regarding the risks and uncontrollability of AI have arisen. In conclusion, vocational students view AI as a practical, human-like tool that improves life, while also recognizing the uncertainties associated with the technology. The findings highlight the dual aspects of AI perceptions in educational settings, merging optimism with caution.

Artificial intelligence can improve recruitment efficiency, but models trained on historical hiring data may reproduce direct and proxy discrimination. This paper presents FairHR-X, an explainable and bias-aware lifecycle framework for human-supervised employee recruitment and selection that integrates predictive modelling, fairness auditing, mitigation, calibration, explainability, human oversight, and continuous monitoring. The framework was evaluated on 10,000 recruiting records regenerated from the CDEI data-generating process, using 6,000 training, 2,000 validation, and 2,000 held-out test observations. Logistic regression achieved the best predictive performance, with a test ROC-AUC of 0.941, PR-AUC of 0.911, and accuracy of 87.35%. The selected fairness-aware configuration, based on intersectional reweighing and Platt calibration, retained 86.45% accuracy and reduced race demographic-parity difference from 0.263 to 0.213, race equalised-odds difference from 0.090 to 0.042, sex demographic-parity difference from 0.163 to 0.119, and the intersectional demographic-parity gap from 0.436 to 0.340. Bootstrap analysis confirmed stable fairness improvements, while SHAP rankings showed high robustness across 1,000 resamples. For external validation, a recruiter-grouped protocol is defined for the 2026 PATHS2INCLUDE dataset comprising 15,036 candidate evaluations from 2,506 recruiters across four European countries. FairHR-X is intended as a transparent decision-support and governance framework rather than an autonomous hiring authority.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The key industry – specific features of oil and gas logistics are the high complexity of supply chains and the multi‑level management system, which determine the quality and characteristics of the communication process between industry participants. An important aspect of the interaction between participants in supply chains is the presence of communication barriers that hinder the effective exchange of information. The study of information logistics flows in the oil and gas sector, the main communication barriers have been identified: organizational, technological, informational, and human. Their substantive characteristics and the degree of their impact on the effectiveness of logistics processes have been clarified, which made it possible to systematize measures to overcome them into two groups: technological and organizational. This also made it possible to justify the use of artificial intelligence technologies as a tool that enables solving complex tasks of managing logistics flows based on high‑speed information processing and multifactor analysis. Identifying the specific features of transactions in the oil and gas industry – the uniqueness of the range of services and the geography of supplies, the high cost, and the significant level of uncertainty – allowed us to conclude that it is advisable to use a predictive support system for negotiations and communications in the context of negotiation processes in oil and gas logistics. This system combines machine learning methods, natural language processing, and predictive analytics into a single platform integrated into the company’s existing digital ecosystem. The mandatory conditions for designing this system are defined as follows: diagnosing the current state of communication processes and identifying problem areas aimed at establishing critically important functional and non-functional requirements for the development of a predictive support system for negotiations and communications. It is proposed to use a multi‑level predictive analytics model that includes three methodological layers: historical analysis – processing of archived data on completed transactions; behavioral analysis – forming indicators based on communication patterns in the current transaction; contextual analysis – taking into account external factors; a substantive description of the methodological layers is provided.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Water distribution systems (WDS) are vital for urban societies by providing clean and safe drinking water. Water utilities have to carefully control the injection of disinfectants such as chlorine to effectively deal with natural contaminants and accidental pollution affecting the drinking water quality. This, however, constitutes a challenging task due to sparse sensor readings, complex system dynamics, and various sources of uncertainty. Despite the importance of this problem, the field lacks realistic, publicly available benchmarks to systematically evaluate and compare automated chlorine injection control strategies. To address this gap, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed for chlorine injection control. It features realistic operational scenarios based on the Cyprus Disinfection-By-Product (CY-DBP) network, a state-of-the-art model derived from a real-world WDS. The benchmark incorporates sparse sensing conditions, realistic water demands, fluctuating source water quality, and multiple wastewater contamination events. Standardized evaluation metrics, focusing on different desiderata, enable consistent and reproducible assessment of chlorine booster station control strategies, facilitating rigorous comparison across methods. To stimulate cross-disciplinary innovation, we also hosted the benchmark as a competition at a leading artificial intelligence (AI) conference, fostering collaboration between the AI and water engineering communities. Although participants proposed diverse data-driven control approaches, none achieved fully satisfactory performance, underscoring the complexity and open challenges of the task. By providing a realistic and demanding testbed, this benchmark establishes a foundation for advancing the research on intelligent and reliable chlorine booster station control strategies.

Using Naturalistic Driving Study data, this study examined how the association between Forward Collision Warning (FCW) activation and perception-reaction time (PRT) varied across driver attention states during car-following. Head-orientation, gaze-direction, and upper-body posture features were used in a Hidden Markov Model to estimate unstable-attention probability over time, and clustering identified three attention-state profiles: stable, fluctuating, and persistently unstable. The stable profile reflected consistently low unstable-state probability, the fluctuating profile reflected frequent shifts in unstable-state probability, and the persistently unstable profile reflected sustained high unstable-state probability. A Gamma generalized estimating equation model was applied to comparable-risk events. The association between FCW activation and PRT showed evidence of variation across attention states, with the largest estimated warning-related reduction observed in the persistently unstable attention state. These findings suggest that considering pre-event attention state may enable a more informative assessment of the support FCW can provide in situations with a greater risk of delayed driver response.

Developing scientific literacy in primary education can be challenging. Teachers often lack the time, scientific domain knowledge, and capacity to provide individualised support and guidance during hands-on science activities. As a result, students may struggle to interpret observations and draw accurate conclusions. To address this, we designed a feedback-enhanced lesson and investigated students’ performance and engagement with optional feedback while developing classification skills using the Solar System as context. Developed within the Minds-On application, the lesson combines hands-on activities with a knowledge-based artificial intelligence approach in which encoded domain knowledge enables automated checking of students’ classifications and error-triggered feedback. Students classify celestial bodies by shape, composition, and orbit using a three-level classification tree. A classroom evaluation with 164 students (ages 10–12), using student-performance and interaction-log data, showed that most successfully engaged with the tasks and navigated their increasing complexity. Performance and interaction data indicated that task difficulty peaked at Level 2, while error rates and engagement decreased at Level 3. Although feedback was available to 89 students following an error, only 25 consulted it at least once, and use was fragmented across classification levels. The small and inconsistent feedback-user subgroup therefore does not allow strong conclusions about feedback effectiveness but provides insight into patterns of feedback uptake and interaction.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Critical infrastructure (CI) operators face an escalating threat environment in which episodic, audit-based compliance verification cannot keep pace with dynamic adversary behavior, converging information technology and operational technology (IT/OT) estates, and expanding regulatory obligations. This article reports a systematic qualitative synthesis examining how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled security posture management can transform compliance with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) from periodic audit into continuous control. Using document analysis and qualitative content analysis of purposively sampled authoritative secondary sources (standards, government publications, regulatory instruments, industry threat reports, and peer-reviewed scholarship), the study develops eight themes: AI applications in CI cybersecurity; continuous monitoring and real-time compliance; CSF alignment; operational and security benefits; organizational and human factors; sector-specific considerations; governance and regulatory implications; and research gaps. Findings indicate that machine learning materially strengthens the Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover functions, compresses the interval between control failure and remediation, and improves audit readiness through continuously generated evidence. However, benefits are contingent on data and telemetry foundations, workforce capability, mitigation of alert fatigue and automation bias, sector-tailored integration with legacy OT, and governance structures that address model risk, explainability, and accountability. The article contributes a five-phase implementation pathway (governance baselining, telemetry consolidation, supervised analytics, conditional automation with human oversight, and continuous assurance) and offers recommendations for operators, policymakers, and researchers. It argues that continuous, AI-assisted compliance is best understood as a sociotechnical control system rather than a purely technological upgrade.

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in higher education assessment has exposed the limits of surveillance- and compliance-based approaches to academic integrity. Institutional responses have largely focused on cheating detection and control, framing integrity as an individual behavioral problem rather than a systemic educational outcome. This chapter argues that such approaches are inadequate in AI-mediated assessment contexts. Drawing on academic integrity research, assessment theory, higher education governance, and AI ethics, it introduces integrity innovation as an alternative framework. Integrity innovation conceptualizes integrity as an outcome of alignment across assessment design, governance, and institutional culture. The chapter shows how AI-based assessment redistributes agency, challenges authorship and originality, and risks deepening global inequities. It positions assessment design and shared responsibility as central to sustaining trust, legitimacy, and the educational mission of higher education in the AI era.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into accounting and auditing has transformed the creation, validation, and application of professional knowledge, raising questions about the legitimacy of algorithmic knowledge in accounting practice. Objective: This study examines the epistemological shift from human judgment to algorithmic knowledge in the implementation of Financial Accounting Standards (Standar Akuntansi Keuangan [SAK]) and Quality Management Systems (Sistem Manajemen Mutu [SMM]). Methods: This study employs a qualitative-interpretive approach through conceptual analysis and an examination of practitioners’ perspectives on the reliability, transparency, explainability, and trustworthiness of AI-assisted decision-making. Results: The results of the study show that AI can improve efficiency, predictive accuracy, and analytical capabilities in modern accounting practices but, at the same time, poses epistemological challenges in the form of limited algorithmic transparency, limited explainability, and the potential erosion of auditors’ professional skepticism. Although the conceptual analysis indicates that AI can positively affect efficiency and predictive accuracy, it also raises epistemic challenges related to transparency, accountability, and the preservation of professional skepticism. The shift from judgment-based knowledge to data-driven inferential knowledge has transformed the traditional epistemic authority held by accountants and auditors. The application of SAK and SMM in the accounting profession has implications for defining professional responsibilities in maintaining the quality of financial reporting and audit processes. Conclusion: This study proposes a human–machine epistemic partnership, in which AI functions as an analytical augmentation tool while accountants and auditors remain the primary epistemic authorities.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding across gynecologic oncology, but most applications remain focused on image interpretation and retrospective prediction rather than direct support of treatment decisions. This review examines how AI is progressing from imaging biomarkers toward multimodal decision-support systems that integrate radiologic, pathologic, molecular, and clinical information. We summarize current applications in ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers, with particular attention to preoperative risk stratification, surgical planning, radiotherapy, systemic treatment selection, treatment-response prediction, and multidisciplinary decision-making. Multimodal approaches are especially promising because they reflect the way clinical decisions are made and may provide greater value than models based on a single data source. However, the current evidence remains dominated by retrospective and often single-center studies, with limited external and prospective validation. Data heterogeneity, domain shift, incomplete multimodal datasets, bias, workflow integration, regulatory requirements, and model monitoring remain important barriers to routine implementation. We therefore outline a stepwise pathway for clinical translation, from robust multicenter validation and prospective human–AI evaluation to clinical-impact studies and post-deployment monitoring. The next phase of AI in gynecologic oncology should prioritize clinically meaningful decisions and measurable patient or workflow benefit rather than incremental gains in predictive performance alone.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can provide individual study support, but the educational significance of its responses depends on how they are examined and used. We develop a conceptual framework comparing Individual Chatbot Interaction and Standard Classroom Interaction, then specify a Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence as a situated implementation of shared AI inquiry. The framework draws on selected scholarship concerning mediated learning, educational dialogue, self-regulation, cognitive engagement, pedagogical agents, and AI literacy. We define the unit of analysis as an interaction episode and distinguish private consultation, shared instruction, and hybrid activities through observable criteria. The tutor is specified as an animated avatar projected by video-mapping onto a static volumetric surface in the classroom; perceived presence and learning are treated as outcomes requiring measurement. The proposed contribution is a design specification linking public AI responses, teacher orchestration, evidence-based scrutiny, and individual reflection. An explanatory pathway connects these conditions to possible cognitive and metacognitive processes, with four propositions and matched comparisons for future evaluation. A projected avatar is neither necessary nor sufficient for collective verification, and its incremental value must be tested against simpler shared interfaces. No empirical effectiveness is claimed. The framework provides a basis for investigating when a situated conversational tutor supports disciplinary understanding and critical AI use.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, including chatbots and virtual tutors, into education has expanded rapidly; however, systematic quantitative analysis of research trends in this field remains limited. Notably, the intellectual foundations of AI agent research lie not in education but in medicine, where AI agents were first extensively deployed and studied in clinical, experimental, and pedagogical contexts. Methods: In this study, a bibliometric analysis of 377 records retrieved from the Web of Science was conducted using VOSviewer to map the evolution, thematic focus, and collaborative networks within this field. Results: The study showed AI agent research originated strongly in healthcare, with educational applications emerging more recently. Key research themes encompassed AI technologies, human–computer interaction, pedagogical applications, and ethical considerations. Collaborative efforts were led by the USA and China, supported by active European and Asian research hubs. The findings revealed a dual narrative of significant benefits for personalized learning and learner well-being alongside persistent challenges such as algorithmic bias and accessibility gaps. Conclusion: To realize the transformative potential of AI in education, future research should prioritize the development of adaptive algorithms, robust ethical frameworks, inclusive design, and interdisciplinary collaboration. By focusing on these areas, the field can work toward overcoming technical, ethical, and logistical barriers, thereby ensuring that AI acts as a sustainable force for equity and excellence in education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Virtual Exchange (VE) has become a key approach in higher education for fostering intercultural competence through online collaboration. However, despite its inclusive framing, many VE initiatives continue to rely on English as a lingua franca or other shared-language arrangements, which may reproduce linguistic hierarchies and unequal participation. This paper examines the potential of AI-supported multilingualism to rethink predominantly monolingual approaches to VE. It argues that while generative AI and translation technologies may reduce communicative barriers and enable broader participation, they do not automatically transform underlying language ideologies or power relations. In doing so, it highlights a tension between accessibility and the interactional work through which intercultural learning occurs. Drawing on Critical Virtual Exchange, relational learning, translanguaging theory, and ethical interculturality, the paper proposes a critical perspective on AI-mediated VE. It further explores how AI may support linguistic equity, multilingual participation, and translanguaging-oriented meaning-making in Virtual Exchange. At the same time, it critically addresses risks such as technological solutionism, linguistic bias in AI systems, and the reinforcement of dominant language ideologies. It concludes that AI-supported VE should be grounded in critical pedagogy and linguistic justice. In this way, VE is reframed not as a site of frictionless communication, but as a relational and ethically accountable educational practice.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Traditional terminology standards often assume that trained users can resolve coexisting translation variants through contextual judgement. As generative artificial intelligence (genAI) and large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate terminology reuse, this raises questions about whether standards encode sufficiently explicit term-selection information for auditable automated selection. This study uses ChatGPT-4o in a prompt-testing procedure to examine whether the WHO’s 2007 and 2022 Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) terminology standards provide sufficient guidance for AI-mediated selection among coexisting English variants. Each sampled term was tested using the same three-prompt sequence: constrained variant selection, brief justification, and a within-session shift from general medical use to possible use in a WHO terminology standard. The model consistently followed the single-choice restriction. Its rationales clustered into four observable justification patterns. Most responses to the third prompt stated that the initial choice would remain unchanged; these responses are reported only as statements produced under this specific sequence. The findings suggest that terminology standards designed for human readability may not provide sufficiently explicit guidance for AI-mediated variant selection. The study therefore proposes a governance stress-test procedure and a minimal set of candidate executable fields for term selection, subject to expert validation and controlled testing.

From Repositories to Knowledge Ecosystems : Artificial Intelligence, Open Science and Adaptive Library Spaces in Indian Higher Education Dr. Amar Nath* Indian academic libraries are undergoing a significant transformation from collection-centred repositories into digitally connected knowledge ecosystems. This transformation is being shaped by the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, expanding national digital infrastructures, artificial intelligence (AI), open-science practices, and changing expectations of learners and researchers. This study examines the emerging knowledge-ecosystem model in Indian higher education through documentary research and secondary-data analysis based on government policies, national digital platforms, institutional reports, and recent scholarly literature. Particular attention is given to three interrelated dimensions: AI-enabled discovery and intelligent library services, open-science infrastructure and scholarly access, and adaptive physical and hybrid learning spaces. The analysis focuses on national initiatives including One Nation One Subscription (ONOS), Shodhganga, the National Digital Library of India (NDLI), and VIDWAN. The official ONOS platform reports more than 6,500 member institutions and more than 1,140 lakh full-text downloads during 2025. Shodhganga crossed the milestone of 600,000 theses in May 2025, while VIDWAN currently reports more than 3.38 lakh academic peers in its verified research directory. These developments demonstrate the increasing importance of interoperable digital infrastructure in supporting research, discovery, collaboration, and lifelong learning. However, technological expansion is accompanied by challenges involving digital inequality, professional competencies, infrastructure, privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, and uneven institutional capacity. The paper proposes a four-layer knowledge-ecosystem framework comprising infrastructure and connectivity; AI and knowledge processing; user-centred services and adaptive spaces; and governance, ethics and professional capacity. The paper argues that the future-ready academic library should no longer be conceptualised merely as a repository of information resources but as an integrated knowledge infrastructure connecting people, content, technology, research, learning and scholarly communication. * Post Graduate Government College, Sector-11, Chandigarh

This article investigates and explores the prototype of a material based project generation system, aiming to transform online DIY content into structured design knowledge for sustainable reuse. Based on an unfinished system developed by the author in his early years, this work reviews the methods of collecting unstructured data from the Internet, extracts key information through lightweight natural language processing, and normalizes it into a unified model suitable for automatic generation. Discussed baseline strategies for retrieving and editing project generation, as well as evaluation metrics that consider constraint satisfaction, feasibility, and user experience. The paper also investigates practical applications in personal creativity support, maker education, and community recycling, supported by initial human in the loop implementation and interactive segmentation code that links material understanding with basic robot operations. The challenges of multimodal alignment, richer constraint modeling, and robust dataset construction have been identified, highlighting opportunities for future integration with digital twins and automated assembly. Although the original system is still incomplete, the study concludes that a practical and impactful pipeline is achievable, demonstrating how artificial intelligence can help users recycle materials more effectively and contribute to sustainable, resource-saving designs.

AI search is changing how users seek information: instead of typing keywords and clicking through links, users increasingly ask complex questions and obtain direct answers on the results page. This shift, together with the rise of “zero-click search” and of chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping the customer experience of information seeking. This paper examines how LLM-based search systems are changing the way users retrieve information online, moving the dominant paradigm from keyword queries and ranked lists of links to direct answers in natural language. The study offers a structured, non-systematic narrative review comparing traditional search engines (represented by Google Search) and conversational AI tools (represented by ChatGPT and GPT-3/3.5-based search tools). It synthesises eight independent studies published between 2023 and 2026: three randomised controlled experiments, two large-scale observational analyses of real-world behaviour and three studies measuring content reliability, complemented by an industry benchmark (Vectara Hallucination Leaderboard). The analysis focuses on five key performance indicators (KPIs): number of queries per task (KPI 1), task success rate/accuracy (KPI 2), total time to task completion (KPI 3), rate of consultation of external sources/outbound clicks as a proxy for cross-verification (KPI 4), and the hallucination rate of AI systems compared with the rate of unreliable results in traditional search (KPI 5). AI systems consistently reduce task completion time, whereas the reduction in the number of queries depends on the task. Accuracy improves only when the generated output is correct; when it is wrong, accuracy drops sharply, consistent with a markedly lower consultation of external sources. The risk of error exists in both paradigms under specific conditions of use. The five KPIs should therefore be read as an interdependent system, with implications for the design of hybrid search tools in human-computer interaction and information retrieval.

Accurate biomechanical modeling is essential for assessing musculoskeletal loading during occupational tasks, but traditional laboratory motion capture is often impractical for field applications. This study developed and evaluated a sensor fusion framework combining flexible wearable sensors with single-view mobile video keypoints for biomechanical modeling of simulated wind turbine maintenance operations. Eighteen healthy participants performed three tasks: symmetric lifting, bolt-torque tensioning, and ladder climbing. Motion was captured simultaneously using 13 BioStamp flexible sensors, a marker-based motion capture system, and mobile video processed with pose detection algorithms. A convolutional neural network was trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation to predict whole-body joint angles referenced to OpenSim inverse kinematics. The fusion model achieved an average RMSE of 9.3°, improving estimation accuracy by 5% compared with the sensor-only model and 21% compared with the video-only model. Findings suggest that combining flexible sensors with video-derived keypoints offers a scalable approach for field-based occupational biomechanics assessment.

Collaborative robots, designed to work alongside humans in shared environments, are transforming manufacturing production lines, enabling partial automation and boosting productivity. But their potential extends beyond these benefits. By implementing anticipatory strategies to prevent workers’ risky behaviours and reduce excessive workloads, collaborative robots can proactively enhance working conditions. For example, they can take on repetitive or strenuous tasks to reduce physical effort or adjust the pace of operations to help alleviate stress levels. Indeed, Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) and Common Mental Disorders (CMDs), which arise from uncontrolled physical and cognitive loads, are major work-related health problems in developed countries, with incommensurate social and economic costs. Collaborative robots can curb the effect of such disorders and help in preserving workers’ health. This Chapter addresses how Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) can be monitored to provide robots with relevant inputs about the human state, and how robots can be employed to improve HFE. Novel strategies are proposed to adapt online robot behaviour to the workers’ psycho-physical state and enhance their well-being and productivity.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) hallucinations raise questions about how users respond to unreliable outputs from a technology on which they depend. Drawing on the cognitive–affective components of the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) framework, this study examines the roles of GAI trust, cognitive dissonance, perceived controllability, and frustration in the relationship between perceived hallucinations and GAI dependence, with GAI literacy and self-efficacy as individual-difference moderators. A between-subjects experiment involved 546 participants who viewed the same GAI dialogue labelled as either containing fabricated information or verified as accurate. Participants in the former condition reported lower trust and perceived controllability, greater cognitive dissonance and frustration, and lower dependence scores. In the parallel model, the indirect associations through trust, controllability, and frustration were negative, whereas the indirect association through cognitive dissonance was positive. Higher GAI literacy weakened the positive controllability–dependence association. The remaining moderation hypotheses were not supported under the directional and multiplicity-adjusted criteria. The findings connect users’ evaluations of unreliable GAI responses with the difficulties they report in regulating their use. They underscore the importance of examining dependence alongside reliability judgements, cognitive conflict, and emotional reactions when assessing the human consequences of GAI hallucinations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity of gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductor manufacturing has exposed the limitations of conventional factory automation, where isolated control systems, centralized decision-making, and human-dependent operations restrict production flexibility, scalability, and long-term optimization. This study proposes a next-generation AI-native architecture for a fully autonomous lights-out GaN semiconductor manufacturing facility that minimizes routine human involvement while enabling continuous, intelligent, and self-optimizing production. In the proposed framework, human participation is intentionally limited to exceptional engineering interventions, major equipment upgrades, regulatory compliance, and strategic decision-making, whereas all routine manufacturing activities are executed autonomously. The proposed architecture integrates distributed Edge AI, autonomous robotic systems, a deterministic industrial communication infrastructure, a real-time Digital Twin, and an AI Factory Operating System (AI-FOS) into a unified operational ecosystem. Unlike conventional smart factories that primarily automate predefined workflows, the proposed system enables perception, reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and continuous process optimization throughout the entire semiconductor production lifecycle, including wafer logistics, epitaxial growth, lithography, etching, metrology, testing, packaging, predictive maintenance, and energy orchestration. A key contribution of this work is the introduction of a distributed twelve-layer cognitive memory architecture, which provides every autonomous robot and intelligent manufacturing node with a common hierarchical decision framework. The architecture prioritizes life safety, environmental protection, anomaly recognition, experiential learning, quality optimization, equipment health monitoring, operational context awareness, asset management, maintenance planning, mission support, environmental signature analysis, and low-priority contextual knowledge. This shared cognitive framework enables consistent decision-making across heterogeneous robotic platforms while supporting continuous learning and knowledge reuse throughout the factory. The proposed architecture represents a shift from automation-centric manufacturing toward cognitive semiconductor production, where the factory operates as an intelligent, self-learning ecosystem rather than a collection of independently automated machines. By combining distributed artificial intelligence, cognitive robotics, Digital Twin technology, and deterministic industrial networking within a unified operating architecture, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for future autonomous semiconductor fabrication facilities designed to achieve high production efficiency, enhanced safety, continuous adaptability, and scalable operation with minimal human intervention. https://dynisos.com/
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can add demographic identities when workplace descriptions leave identity unspecified. We audited nine live model configurations using 20 experimental and five control phrases, with 50 stateless generations per model–phrase cell at temperature 1.0 (11,250 responses). The experimental conditions bundled role content with communicative register: authority/resource-control phrases were direct or directive, whereas coordination/assistance phrases were reporting, deferential, or permission-seeking. The design therefore estimates a role-and-register contrast, not a causal effect of occupational status alone. Both conditions were majority female: full-grid attribution was 63.58% female, 35.89% male, 0.47% nonbinary, and 0.07% unparsed in the authority/directive condition, versus 92.62%, 6.04%, 1.20%, and 0.13%, respectively, in the support/deferential condition. Model risk differences ranged from − 12.2 to + 93.6 percentage points. A Paule–Mandel random-effects synthesis showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 98.6% on the log-odds scale; 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio, 0.014–63,659), so no stable common model effect is claimed. A cross-classified block bootstrap retaining 50-response cells estimated an aggregate male-attribution gap of 29.9 points (95% CI, 6.0–55.6). Name entropy diagnostics documented substantial within-cell repetition. Control mismatches were predominantly explicit model outputs rather than parser failures; excluding models below 80% control agreement did not reverse the aggregate gap. Name-based race inference is confined to a reliability appendix. The results identify heterogeneous demographic defaults under this prompt bundle and motivate crossed role-by-register experiments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The targeted discovery of inorganic materials remains challenging due to the vastness of compositional design spaces and the high cost of exhaustive screening. Task-specific generative artificial intelligence represents a particularly efficient alternative to screening, yet demands tedious collection of training data before providing real benefit. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently shown tremendous potential for the targeted generation of single, optimal materials compositions without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. However, it is unclear whether LLMs generally pose an advantage compared to specialized generative models, in particular in large design spaces. Here, we demonstrate that such models are capable of covering entire regions of the targeted property space effectively and systematically. Using Elpasolite materials as an established benchmark for generative tasks in large chemical spaces, we find that an iterative prompt-and-response framework is able to recover on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. This performance, driven mainly by iterative in-context learning, surpasses the generative abilities of previous, task-specific models. Our results establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows.

This article theoretically examines the pedagogical and methodological opportunities, organizational mechanisms, and didactic conditions for developing students’ independent learning activities in vocational education institutions through the use of generative artificial intelligence technologies. The research findings present methodological recommendations developed on the basis of theoretical analysis and substantiate the need for further experimental studies to determine their empirical effectiveness.

The public release of ChatGPT presents language education with both advantages and challenges. Being widely available and readily producing texts at user's command, it is an especially useful resource in ESL writing. However, to be able to leverage it effectively for that purpose, we need to understand the writing micro-processes surrounding its use. To this end, this study investigates, through an experimental design, writing micro-processes along with writing outcomes, and perceptions of 12 ESL writers across three writing conditions. The data included interviews, questionnaires as well as essay grades and screen recordings. Two of the three conditions involved the use of ChatGPT. The results indicate that the majority of participants favored the ChatGPT- assisted conditions and noted its role in aiding idea generation. Despite this preference, some participants noted that ChatGPT-produced texts felt robotic and lacked a human touch. We found no statistically significant differences across the three conditions in the participants' essays. Most notably, our analysis identified distinct clusters of writing micro-processes associated with the ChatGPT conditions, suggesting that generative AI tools can influence writing behaviors although the link to outcomes is not straightforward. These findings provide insights into the potential benefits and limitations of using AI tools in writing tasks. The article discusses areas for further research to enhance the integration of AI into ESL writing education.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redefining marketing communication by extending the discipline beyond human-driven creativity into a data-supported, emotionally responsive, and context-aware domain. Unlike traditional AI focused on automation and analytics, generative AI enables personalized content creation, immersive brand storytelling, and adaptive consumer engagement. This chapter examines generative AI as a creative paradigm through the lenses of neuromarketing, cognitive psychology, and consumer behavior, highlighting how large language models, visual generators, and multimodal systems support “machine creativity.” It further discusses measurement approaches like EEG, eye-tracking, and AI-based sentiment analysis that may be used to assess emotional impact. Ethical concerns such as privacy, consent, and transparency are discussed in light of emerging governance frameworks. The chapter concludes by considering future integration in VR, AR, and metaverse environments and emphasizes a collaborative balance between human creativity and AI-driven innovation.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming entrepreneurship by helping entrepreneurs generate ideas, analyze information, create content, develop business models, support marketing, and make decisions. This review examines the growing role of GenAI in entrepreneurial activities, with a focus on opportunity recognition, creativity, innovation, SMEs, emerging economies, and responsible AI use. GenAI can reduce resource constraints and provide affordable support to small businesses, but challenges such as inaccurate information, overdependence, privacy concerns, and unequal digital skills remain. The article highlights the importance of human–AI collaboration and introduces the concept of AI entrepreneurial capability, which includes AI literacy, effective prompting, evaluation of AI outputs, decision-making, and responsible use of AI. The review concludes that future entrepreneurship should focus not only on using AI to generate more opportunities but also on improving the quality, sustainability, and responsible development of those opportunities.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders are a major occupational health concern, and REBA is widely used to evaluate postural risk. The role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in REBA scoring remains insufficiently examined.ObjectiveTo explore REBA scoring differences between a certified human ergonomist and three generative AI systems under controlled multimodal input conditions.MethodsSeventy-seven anonymized posture images from four task categories were evaluated by a human reference evaluator and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Wrtn. Identical images and standardized posture descriptors were provided to the AI systems. REBA scores were compared using repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc comparisons.ResultsSignificant rater, body-part, and rater × body-part effects were observed. Wrtn generated comparatively higher trunk and wrist scores and lower scores for the lower arm, Gemini generated comparatively higher Final REBA scores, and ChatGPT produced comparatively lower scores across several body regions.ConclusionsGenerative AI systems showed systematic body-region-specific differences in REBA scoring relative to the human reference evaluator. These exploratory findings indicate the need for further validation and expert oversight before AI-assisted REBA assessment is used in workplace practice.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the implications of generative artificial intelligence for assessment practices, academic integrity and quality assurance in South African higher education institutions. As AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, SciSpace, Gemini, and Copilot become embedded in teaching, learning and assessment, they offer opportunities to enhance efficiency, feedback and assessment design while raising ethical concerns about misconduct, authorship, transparency and assessment validity. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour and the Utilitarian Theory of Ethics, the chapter adopts a conceptual and critical approach to analyse how the literature portrays academics' and students' perceptions, adoption and justification of the ethical or unethical use of generative artificial intelligence in assessment contexts. Particular attention is given to challenges surrounding originality, intellectual property, and authenticity, which, in turn, have implications for assessment outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Breast symmetry and harmony remain challenging goals in aesthetic breast surgery. Preoperative marking is fundamental for planning; however, most techniques rely on nipple–areola complex (NAC) distances and subjective visual assessment, often neglecting thoracic width, height, and the true breast footprint. A geometric framework based on harmonic proportions can help standardize preoperative planning and may improve the reproducibility of breast markings. Methods A two-dimensional geometric template was developed by integrating constant anatomical references (sternum, clavicles, axillary and acromial lines, and umbilicus) with proportional relationships derived from aesthetic and anthropometric studies. The template was calibrated for each patient’s using thoracic width and height and was designed to be superimposed on standardized frontal photographs. It guides the NAC position, breast width, upper pole contour, and inframammary fold level. The model was applied in mastopexy and reduction mammaplasty as a preoperative planning and postoperative photographic overlay comparison, as well as a visual aid in resident teaching sessions. Results The template was easily incorporated into daily practice using standard clinical photographs and simple digital overlays. Geometric gridlines and proportional curves allowed visualization of the NAC position, breast symmetry, and contour in relation to thoracic dimensions. Repeated overlays facilitated the longitudinal comparison of breast position and shape. During teaching sessions, the template was used as a visual aid to facilitate resident understanding of the geometric relationships between thoracic anatomy, the breast footprint, and marking decisions. Conclusions This innovative geometric template offers a simple, visually intuitive tool for standardizing preoperative marking and supporting postoperative photographic overlay comparisons in breast surgeries. It is inexpensive, compatible with existing photographic workflows, and may support training and future digital or artificial intelligence integration. Prospective studies are needed to quantify the impact of these factors on aesthetic outcomes and learning curves. Level of Evidence V This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

Background: The escalating burden and distinct clinical manifestations of depression in women demand innovative psychiatric frameworks. Exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, the limitations of traditional care have catalyzed the integration of artificial intelligence into digital mental health, providing scalable, gender-sensitive solutions for personalized prediction and intervention. Objective: This study employs a quantitative bibliometric approach to objectively present the overarching research landscape, collaboration networks, and emerging trends at the intersection of AI and women's depression over a decade-long period (2016–2026). Methods:A comprehensive literature retrieval was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases for the period from January 1, 2016, to August 31, 2026. Advanced visualization tools, specifically CiteSpace and VOSviewer, were utilized to systematically analyze temporal publication trends, spatial distribution (countries/institutions), co-authorship networks, and core research hotspots. Results:Research output exhibited a well-defined phased growth, marked by a dramatic 56% surge in 2021 and culminating in a peak of 1,620 publications in 2025. The United States and China led global productivity, with the University of California emerging as the top-contributing institution and Bin Hu as the most prolific author. Core research clusters encompass the utilization of multimodal deep learning models for early predictive analytics and AI-augmented Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) through advanced natural language processing.Targeted conditions, notably postpartum depression, remain prominent clinical focus areas. Conclusion: The field is unequivocally transitioning from a phase of explosive quantitative growth into a stage of specialized clinical consolidation and personalized intervention. While AI architectures offer transformative potential for predicting and managing women's depression, future scientific investments must prioritize mitigating algorithmic biases across diverse female populations and fostering deeper cross-institutional collaborations to support sustainable clinical innovations.

AI-enabled assessment technologies are increasingly used by higher education institutions to protect academic integrity, scale online assessment and respond strategically to generative artificial intelligence. This paper examines how online proctoring, automated scoring, AI writing detection, and learning analytics risk flagging reshape institutional governance, stakeholder trust, and assessment strategy in higher education business ecosystems. Using a systematic-narrative review approach informed by PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, the study synthesises peer-reviewed literature and authoritative policy guidance published between 2015 and 2025. The analysis is organised around an integrated theoretical framework that combines assessment validity, academic integrity values, algorithmic accountability, and ecosystem strategy. The findings show that AI-enabled assessment can support identity verification, monitoring capacity, workflow triage and timely feedback when deployed as human-governed decision support rather than automated adjudication. However, over-reliance on surveillance and detection creates strategic risks: false positives, bias against linguistically diverse students, privacy intrusion, opaque decision-making, weakened due process and construct distortion when assessments measure surveillance compliance instead of intended learning outcomes. The review further shows that institutional legitimacy depends less on the technical promise of tools and more on governance capability, including proportionality, transparency, contestability, equity auditing, privacy protection and authentic assessment redesign. The paper contributes to business ecosystem and strategy scholarship by positioning academic integrity technology as a strategic governance issue within higher education service ecosystems. It recommends integrity-by-design, cross-functional AI governance, vendor accountability and assessment strategies that preserve fairness, validity and stakeholder trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human–AI decision authority is analyzed in relation to changes in relative competence and decision risk, taking institutional oversight capacity into account. The proposed Co-Agency Equilibrium Theory (CAET) and Co-Agency Equilibrium Model (CAEM) offer a sociotechnical perspective on humans and AI working as co-agents with varying shares of decision authority. CAET connects the four dimensions, including relative competence, moral salience, irreversibility, and institutional context, with the human authority share and Accountability Gap between delegated risk and human vigilance capability. CAEM combines a logistic policy surface, accountability gap feedback and a gradual adjustment of the human control level, with a switch to full human control if moral salience or irreversibility reaches or exceeds the corresponding threshold. Monotonicity and convergence results are obtained for the model under certain assumptions, and comparative statics illustrate the impact of threshold choices on the escalation region. Simulations in which moral salience and irreversibility are varied separately show the effects of threshold choices on the timing of human takeover under more cautious and more risk-tolerant authority-allocation policies. The framework serves as a blueprint for designing human-AI control logic with normative constraints and deciding on the right level of AI authority based on performance, stakes and domain-specific accountability considerations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Nanoparticles are increasingly investigated in forensic science for latent fingermark development, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), trace drug and explosive detection, gunshot-residue analysis, surface-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (SALDI-MS), and biological-evidence processing. However, conventional nanoparticle synthesis may involve hazardous reducing agents, organic solvents, energy-intensive conditions, and surface contaminants that can affect environmental sustainability and analytical compatibility. Green synthesis uses plant extracts, microorganisms, algae, or purified biomolecules as reducing and stabilizing systems, offering a potentially safer and more sustainable alternative. Main body This review critically examines plant-, microbial-, algal-, and biomolecule-mediated synthesis of metal and metal-oxide nanoparticles, with particular attention to reaction mechanisms, process variables, extract standardization, batch-to-batch reproducibility, scalability, and storage stability. The complementary roles and limitations of ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, dynamic light scattering, zeta-potential analysis, electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface-area analysis are evaluated. Forensic applications are assessed according to nanoparticle composition, substrate compatibility, analytical sensitivity, selectivity, detection limit, reproducibility, real-sample testing, and comparison with established methods. Particular emphasis is placed on latent fingermarks, SERS-based detection, SALDI-MS, gunshot residue, forensic toxicology, questioned documents, and biological evidence. The review also examines sustainability, biosafety, regulatory requirements, and the potential roles of artificial intelligence, machine learning, portable instrumentation, and smartphone-assisted detection. Conclusion Green-synthesized nanoparticles offer promising surface properties and analytical functions for forensic science, but most reported applications remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Variability in biological materials, incomplete mechanistic characterization, limited quantitative benchmarking, and insufficient validation using realistic casework samples currently restrict routine implementation. Progress toward operational use will require standardized synthesis and quality-control procedures, transparent performance reporting, interlaboratory studies, environmental and toxicological assessment, and validation consistent with accredited forensic laboratory requirements.
topics: Gold and Silver Nanoparticles Synthesis and Applications

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education; however, most instructional applications emphasizeanswer generation rather than mathematical reasoning and critical verification of AI-generated mathematical solutions. The current study examined the effectiveness of the Guided AI Integration Model (GAIIM), a verification-oriented instructional framework that utilizes AI for verification of students’ algebraic problem-solving within a problem-solving context. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 86 undergraduate mathematics education students using a randomized pretest-posttest control group classroom design. During the 12-week intervention, students in the experimental group engaged in GAIIM-based instruction involving independent problem-solving, AI-generated solution comparison, error detection and justification, error resolution, and reflective verification, while the control group received conventional algebra instruction. Qualitative data were subsequently collected from 10 purposively selected students through semi-structured interviews and analyzed thematically to explain and elaborate on the quantitative findings. Students in the GAIIM group demonstrated significantly higher posttest performance in algebraic problem-solving, error detection, and error resolution after controlling for pretest scores. Qualitative findings further revealed stepwise verification, iterative engagement with AI feedback, conditional trust in AI-generated responses, and difficulties interpreting and correcting AI-generated mathematical reasoning. The findings suggest that structured AI-supported verification can support students’ algebraic problem-solving and error-verification performance.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Sustainability can be conceptualized as three interlinked aspects: economic; social; and natural capital. In this chapter we will examine what is required for each of these aspects from a human factors and ergonomics perspective to enable sustainability in human-robotic systems. When looking at the economic and social capital nexus it is important to take into account issues of safety and the future roles of humans in robotic systems. This includes issues such as skills, training, resilience, and employment status of the humans. Furthermore, the possibilities arising from advanced social robotics also requires an examination of issues such as privacy, trust, and understandability. When looking at the economic and natural capital nexus it is necessary to consider aspects such as the materials used to produce, maintain, and deconstruct robotic systems as well as the eco-efficiencies and eco-effectiveness that can be obtained from including robotics in human systems. Such an examination requires a consideration of the diverse impact of robotic systems in different geographical communities, and among regions with different economic development status. The social and natural capital nexus requires us to evaluate when and where to invest in human-robotic systems, but also when and where to resist such developments. Finally, we consider the HFE values that are needed to help develop a more sustainable approach to the development of human-robotic systems.

Hospital operational artificial intelligence (AI) can reduce visible task time, but postdeployment affordability also depends on work transferred to staff, technical teams, budgets, and vendors. This focused structured narrative Mini Review examined hidden labor, monitoring and maintenance, and exit or replacement burdens after real hospital AI deployment, with implications for resource-constrained Chinese hospitals. Reconciliation of retained candidates produced a 23-record analytic inventory, including 15 reports grouped into 12 primary deployment clusters; other records supplied adjacent, contextual or governance evidence. Exhaustive coverage is not claimed. Evidence was classified by burden domain, bearer, and three outcome levels: observed work, labor value or opportunity cost, and budget or cash expenditure. Human verification, correction, adaptation, data upkeep, and coordination persisted in several deployments, although one controlled study found no significant increase in review burden. Monitoring required continuing ownership and remediation capacity. Direct operational-AI permanent-exit evidence remained limited to one hospital lifecycle case. Chinese reports identify workflow responsibilities but do not establish AI lifecycle affordability in resource-constrained hospitals. The proposed Pilot, Scale, Modify, Share, and Stop framework comprises locally testable management propositions, not validated thresholds or Chinese cost estimates. Prospective studies should measure burdens across clinical, administrative, technical, financial, vendor, and regional actors.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As the population of older adults grows, home robots may help address daily living challenges associated with mobility, cognitive change, health management, and social isolation. This study examined deployment requirements for assistive home robots from a human factors and ergonomics perspective by evaluating the Stretch mobile manipulator with older adults and community care staff in a simulated life-plan community apartment. Using demonstrations and semi-structured interviews, we assessed perceptions of usability, acceptance, and task relevance. Findings showed strong interest in support for safety, object retrieval, medication and hydration reminders, telehealth access, exercise adherence, and social connection. Participants emphasized design requirements critical to deployment, including intuitive multimodal interaction, reliable operation in unstructured home environments, personalization over time, and early stakeholder involvement. The results highlight how human-centered evaluation can identify deployment needs and guide the safe, effective integration of home robots to support independence, overall well-being, and quality of life among older adults.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI). The goal of machine learning generally is to understand the structure of data and fit that data into models that can be understood and utilized by people. Although machine learning is a field within computer science, it differs from traditional computational approaches. In traditional computing, algorithms are sets of explicitly programmed instructions used by computers to calculate or problem solve. Machine learning algorithms instead allow for computers to train on data inputs and use statistical analysis in order to output values that fall within a specific range. Because of this, machine learning facilitates computers in building models from sample data in order to automate decision making processes based on data inputs.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs)-generated texts become increasingly similar to human writing. The purpose of this study was to examine (1) how individuals distinguish between human-written and LLM-generated texts, focusing on their judgment strategies; (2) the relationship between judgment strategies and detection accuracy; and (3) the interaction effects of gender, age, and frequency of large language model (LLM) use. Methods Participants were asked to judge whether the given texts (e.g., public comments) were written by LLMs or humans and to explain their reasoning using open-ended questions. The public comments were written by humans and generated using seven LLMs (ChatGPT [4o and o1], Claude3.5, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Llama3.1, and Perplexity). First, we classified participants’ explanations of reasoning related to judgments into types using BERT-based clustering (i.e., Sentence-BERT and hierarchical cluster analysis). Results BERT-based clustering suggested four interpretable clusters. Based on their characteristic patterns, we interpreted these clusters as four hypothetical judgment strategy types and tentatively proposed that they form a conceptual continuum: (1) Unsubstantiated intuition, (2) Stylistic-Cue, (3) Syntactic-Cue, and (4) Higher-Order Pattern Recognition (HOPR). A hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression analysis revealed that the detection accuracy varied across judgment types, with the HOPR type achieving relatively higher performance than the other strategy types, although its detection accuracy remained near the chance level.
